title: “BUT ABRAHAM HAD MORE THAN ONE WIFE…” — THE BIBLE VERSES PEOPLE USE TO DEFEND POLYGAMY MAY ACTUALLY BE WARNING US ABOUT IT
paragraphs:
“BUT ABRAHAM HAD MORE THAN ONE WIFE…” — THE BIBLE VERSES PEOPLE USE TO DEFEND POLYGAMY MAY ACTUALLY BE WARNING US ABOUT IT
Can Christians Use Old Testament Polygamy to Defend Modern Polygamy? What Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon, Genesis—and Jesus Himself—Actually Reveal About God’s Design for Marriage
There is an argument that sounds devastating until you actually open the Bible.
“Abraham had more than one woman.”
“Jacob had Leah and Rachel.”
“David had multiple wives.”
“Solomon had hundreds.”
“So how can Christians say polygamy is wrong?”
At first, it sounds like someone has discovered an embarrassing contradiction Christians have been trying to hide.
But stay with me.
Because buried underneath this question is something much bigger than marriage.
It is a question about how you read the Bible.
And if you get this wrong, you can eventually make Scripture defend almost anything.
The Bible tells us that Noah became drunk.
It tells us that Abraham lied about Sarah.
It tells us that Jacob deceived.
It tells us that Judah slept with a woman he thought was a prostitute.
It tells us that Moses murdered an Egyptian.
It tells us that David committed adultery and arranged a man's death.
It tells us that Peter denied Jesus.
It tells us that Judas betrayed Him.
Yet nobody opens the Bible, finds Judas betraying Christ, and concludes:
“Judas did it, therefore betrayal must be biblical.”
Why?
Because Scripture describing something is not the same thing as Scripture approving something.
And that distinction changes everything.
The Bible is brutally honest about its heroes because the Bible is not ultimately a book about heroic men.
It is a book about a holy God rescuing sinful people.
That is why Scripture does not airbrush Abraham.
It does not sanitize Jacob.
It does not protect David's reputation.
It does not hide Solomon's collapse.
God allows us to see their faith...
and their failures.
Their obedience...
and their compromises.
Their victories...
and the wreckage they created when they stopped trusting Him.
So when someone says, “Polygamy is in the Bible,” the Christian does not need to panic.
Yes.
It is.
So are adultery, murder, idolatry, deception, incest, drunkenness, betrayal, war, jealousy and human rebellion.
The real question has never been:
“Does this behavior appear somewhere in Scripture?”
The real question is:
“What does the whole counsel of Scripture reveal about God's design?”
And for marriage, the trail does not begin with Abraham.
It begins before Abraham.
Before Moses.
Before Israel.
Before kings.
Before human culture had centuries to normalize its brokenness.
It begins in Eden.
Genesis 2:24 preserves these words:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Al-ken ya'azov-ish et-aviv ve'et-immo, vedavaq be'ishto, vehayu levasar echad.
In straightforward sense:
“Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother, clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.”
Listen carefully to the language.
וְדָבַק — vedavaq.
He clings.
He cleaves.
He binds himself.
בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ — be'ishto.
To his wife.
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד — vehayu levasar echad.
And they become one flesh.
One flesh.
Not because human beings eventually invented an idealized Victorian marriage arrangement.
Not because Paul suddenly became culturally conservative.
Not because the early church needed a convenient social structure.
This pattern is embedded in the creation narrative itself.
And centuries later, when religious leaders attempted to drag Jesus into a controversy over marriage, Christ did something extraordinarily important.
He went back to Genesis.
He did not begin with Abraham.
He did not begin with Jacob.
He did not say, “Well, David had several wives, so let's use David's household as our definition.”
He returned to creation.
Jesus said that the Creator made them “male and female,” and then invoked Genesis: a man leaves father and mother, holds fast to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
The Greek tradition of Matthew 19:5 expresses the crucial phrase:
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
kai esontai hoi duo eis sarka mian.
“The two shall become one flesh.”
οἱ δύο — hoi duo.
The two.
σάρκα μίαν — sarka mian.
One flesh.
Then Jesus draws the conclusion:
They are no longer two, but one flesh.
What God has joined together, man must not separate.
That matters enormously.
Because Jesus gives us a way of reading marital history in Scripture.
He distinguishes between God's creation intention and arrangements that arose within a fallen world.
In that same discussion, Jesus confronts divorce by saying Moses permitted something because of human hardness of heart, but then Christ says words that should make every serious Bible reader stop:
“From the beginning it was not so.”
There it is.
Sometimes the question is not merely:
“What occurred under the old covenant?”
Sometimes the deeper question is:
“What was God's intention from the beginning?”
That distinction destroys a lot of careless Bible arguments.
Because if every Old Testament practice automatically represented God's timeless ideal, then merely finding something practiced by a patriarch or king would settle the matter.
But Jesus Himself does not read Scripture that way.
He takes us back.
Back through Moses.
Back through Israel.
Back through the patriarchs.
Back through centuries of human accommodation and failure.
Back...
to the beginning.
And what do we find?
One man.
One woman.
One covenantal union.
One flesh.
Then sin enters the world.
And watch what happens.
The first explicit polygamist named in Scripture is not Abraham.
It is Lamech.
Genesis 4:19 tells us:
“Lamech took two wives.”
That sentence appears in the lineage of Cain, within a narrative increasingly marked by violence and human self-exaltation.
Lamech eventually boasts about killing a man.
This does not by itself mean that every action Lamech performs is automatically condemned simply because Lamech performed it.
But it should immediately make us cautious about presenting his household as the restoration of Eden.
Then comes Abraham.
God had promised him descendants.
Years passed.
Sarah remained barren.
The promise seemed impossible.
And Genesis 16 records one of the most painfully human moments in Scripture.
Sarah gives Hagar to Abraham.
Abraham sleeps with her.
Hagar conceives.
And almost immediately...
the house fractures.
Genesis says that when Hagar realized she had conceived, her mistress became contemptible in her eyes.
Sarah becomes angry.
Abraham withdraws from responsibility.
Hagar is mistreated.
She runs.
Think about that.
The Bible does not present this arrangement as a glowing advertisement for expanding marriage.
It shows a household bleeding.
Jealousy.
Power.
Pain.
Humiliation.
Conflict.
A vulnerable woman fleeing into the wilderness.
And yet...
God sees Hagar.
That is one of the most beautiful parts of the story.
Human beings created the mess.
God entered the wilderness.
Hagar encounters the God who sees her.
Grace walked into the consequences of human failure.
But grace entering the wreckage does not mean God endorses whatever created the wreckage.
Please hear that.
God's mercy toward people living inside broken situations should never be confused with God's approval of every decision that produced those situations.
That is important far beyond this discussion.
Somebody reading this may already have made choices you deeply regret.
Sexual choices.
Marriage choices.
Relationship choices.
Maybe your family story is complicated.
Maybe you discovered Christ after the damage had already happened.
Maybe there are children involved.
Maybe there are wounds that cannot simply be erased by pretending yesterday never existed.
The Gospel is not telling you that you are beyond redemption.
Jesus specializes in meeting people inside stories that have become complicated.
But redemption does not require us to rename brokenness as righteousness.
Grace tells the truth...
and then refuses to abandon the sinner.
Keep reading Genesis.
Jacob loves Rachel.
But through deception and complicated cultural arrangements, Leah becomes his wife too.
Rachel enters the marriage afterward.
Then servants become involved in childbearing.
And what grows inside this household?
Competition.
Jealousy.
Heartbreak.
Favoritism.
Women measuring their worth through children.
Sisters competing for affection.
Children growing up inside a family fractured by preferential love.
Eventually Joseph, the favored son of the favored woman, becomes the object of such intense resentment that his brothers sell him.
Again, Scripture does not stop every few verses to write:
It does something more powerful.
It lets you live inside the house.
It lets you hear Leah's ache.
It lets you feel Rachel's desperation.
It lets you watch Jacob's favoritism.
It lets you see what children absorb when adults normalize relational disorder.
The Bible does not need a laugh track telling you when something is tragic.
Sometimes the consequences are the commentary.
Then there is Hannah.
Elkanah had two wives: Hannah and Peninnah.
And what do we find?
Rivalry.
Provocation.
Tears.
First Samuel describes Hannah being tormented so severely that she weeps and cannot eat.
Again...
a divided household.
Again...
two women living within one man's marital structure.
Again...
pain.
Then David.
The man after God's own heart.
And this is where people sometimes become careless.
David loved God.
David also sinned catastrophically.
Those two truths are both in the Bible.
His inclusion in the story of redemption does not transform every choice he made into a commandment.
David accumulated wives.
Then he desired Bathsheba.
She belonged to Uriah.
David took her.
When pregnancy threatened exposure, David attempted concealment.
Eventually Uriah was placed where battle would kill him.
Desire became adultery.
Adultery became deception.
Deception became bloodshed.
And the prophet Nathan confronted the king.
That is not Scripture saying, “Kings may construct whatever sexual arrangements they desire.”
That is Scripture exposing what happens when a powerful man begins treating women, bodies and marriages as possessions available to his appetite.
And before Israel even had kings, Deuteronomy 17:17 had warned concerning the king:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים
Velo yarbeh-lo nashim.
“He shall not multiply wives for himself.”
Why?
The text continues with the danger:
So that his heart does not turn away.
Then Solomon arrives.
And Solomon practically becomes a living commentary on that warning.
First Kings tells us Solomon loved many foreign women.
His household eventually included seven hundred wives of royal status and three hundred concubines.
Then comes the sentence nobody defending modern polygamy with Solomon should ignore:
His wives turned away his heart.
The man famous for wisdom became foolish in the very place God had warned Israel's kings.
Solomon built places of worship for false gods.
His divided romantic loyalties became entangled with divided worship.
And suddenly this conversation is no longer only about how many people someone can marry.
It is about the human heart.
Because the deepest danger in sexual compromise is not merely that it may complicate your relationships.
It can compete with your worship.
Anything you refuse to surrender to Christ eventually begins demanding something from you that belongs to Christ.
This is why Christians must be extraordinarily careful when saying:
“But someone in the Bible did it.”
The Bible contains saints whose lives sometimes function as warnings.
Abraham teaches us faith...
and shows us what fear can do.
Jacob teaches us perseverance...
and shows us what deception can do.
David teaches us worship...
and shows us what unchecked lust and power can do.
Solomon teaches us wisdom...
and demonstrates that possessing wisdom does not guarantee obeying it.
Peter teaches us courage...
and shows us how quickly fear can make a disciple deny the Lord he loves.
Scripture's heroes do not save us.
Jesus does.
And that brings us to the center of everything.
Christ.
Christian marriage cannot finally be defined by asking what Abraham tolerated, what Jacob inherited, what David practiced or what Solomon accumulated.
Christian marriage must ultimately be understood through God's creation design as reaffirmed by Jesus Christ and illuminated by the apostolic witness.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5 that marriage mysteriously points beyond itself.
A husband and wife become a living picture of something greater:
Christ and His Church.
Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 again.
The man leaves father and mother.
He holds fast to his wife.
The two become one flesh.
Then Paul says:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
Marriage is therefore not merely an arrangement for romance, reproduction, companionship, property, sexual access or social stability.
In Christian theology, marriage becomes an icon of covenant.
Christ.
And His Bride.
The Bridegroom giving Himself sacrificially.
The Bride belonging faithfully to Him.
Covenant love.
Sacrificial love.
Exclusive devotion.
Faithfulness.
That is why adultery is spiritually serious.
That is why sexual faithfulness matters.
That is why marriage cannot simply be reconstructed around whatever arrangement human desire finds attractive.
Marriage tells a story.
And Christians do not own the story.
God does.
Even Paul's language regarding church leadership reinforces the expectation of marital fidelity.
In 1 Timothy 3:2, an overseer is described with the Greek expression:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
mias gynaikos andra.
Literally, the expression carries the idea of being “a man of one woman,” commonly translated “husband of one wife,” with some translations emphasizing faithfulness to one's wife.

Scholars discuss precisely how the idiom should be applied in questions such as remarriage and qualifications for church office, so we should not pretend that one phrase resolves every conceivable marital question.
But it certainly does not provide support for celebrating plural wives as the Christian marital ideal.
And here is where intellectual honesty matters.
The Old Testament does contain laws addressing situations involving multiple wives.
Exodus 21 addresses obligations in a complicated marital household.
Deuteronomy 21 addresses inheritance when a man has two wives.
Someone may say:
“There. God regulated it. Therefore God approved it.”
But regulation and idealization are not identical.
Biblical law sometimes speaks into broken social realities in order to restrain exploitation, establish justice and protect vulnerable people.
A law telling a man what he owes a woman does not necessarily mean the social arrangement producing the problem represents creation's highest ideal.
Jesus' own treatment of divorce demonstrates that distinction.
A Mosaic provision can address human brokenness without replacing Eden as the theological foundation of marriage.
This is why we must read individual texts inside the whole biblical story.
Creation.
Fall.
Israel.
Christ.
Church.
New creation.
When you follow that movement, the trajectory becomes clearer.
The question is not whether ancient societies practiced polygamy.
They obviously did.
The question is whether Christians today can point to those narratives and say:
“Therefore God has given us a positive model to reproduce.”
That case is exceedingly difficult to sustain from the Bible's own movement.
Especially when Jesus takes us directly back to “the two” becoming “one flesh.”
But perhaps you are still thinking:
“What about Abraham? God blessed him.”
Yes.
And this may be the most beautiful answer of all.
God blessed deeply imperfect people.
That is Christianity.
Abraham's failures did not overpower God's promise.
Jacob's dysfunction did not terminate God's covenant.
David's sexual sin did not make repentance impossible.
Peter's denial did not prevent restoration.
Why?
Because the Bible is not the story of flawless people climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of God descending into human wreckage to rescue sinners.
Eventually...
God Himself entered our world.
Jesus Christ.
Born into the human family.
Tempted, yet without sin.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
The Bridegroom gave Himself for His Bride.
Not because she was spotless.
But to make her holy.
That is Gospel love.
And suddenly marriage becomes far more challenging than merely asking:
“How many wives am I technically allowed to have?”
The Gospel asks:
“How much of yourself are you willing to crucify in order to love faithfully?”
Can you lay down lust?
Can you lay down entitlement?
Can you lay down secret messages?
Can you lay down pornography?
Can you lay down fantasies?
Can you lay down emotional affairs?
Can you lay down the hunger to be desired by everyone?
Can you lay down the part of you that wants covenant benefits without covenant boundaries?
Because maybe the greatest threat to Christian marriage today is not somebody publicly announcing three wives.
Maybe it is people claiming one spouse while carrying ten secret lovers in their minds.
Maybe it is the husband who would loudly condemn polygamy but privately consumes pornography every night.
Maybe it is the wife who remains physically married while emotionally belonging to somebody else.
Maybe it is the Christian who argues passionately for “biblical marriage” while refusing to forgive, refusing to serve, refusing to repent and refusing to love sacrificially.
Jesus does not merely want us to win an argument about marriage.
He wants our hearts.
All of them.
That is where this article becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is easy to discuss Solomon's thousand women.
It is harder to discuss the one person in your messages your spouse doesn't know about.
It is easy to condemn David.
It is harder to confess the fantasy you keep feeding.
It is easy to explain Genesis in Hebrew.
It is harder to obey Genesis when covenant becomes costly.
It is easy to type “one man, one woman.”
It is harder to become a faithful man.
A faithful woman.
A faithful disciple.
Maybe someone reading this has already failed.
Maybe badly.
Maybe your marriage is wounded because of something you did.
Maybe your spouse betrayed you.
Maybe you are carrying shame from sexual sin.
Maybe you entered relationships before you understood Christ.
Maybe your family history looks nothing like Eden.
Maybe you are reading this while wondering whether Jesus could possibly want somebody with your history.
Look at the cross.
That is your answer.
Christianity is not the announcement that respectable people have successfully avoided scandal.
Christianity is the announcement that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The cross does not minimize sin.
The cross proves how serious sin is.
But the empty tomb proves sin does not get the final word for those who belong to Christ.
Repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
Repentance is turning around because Someone better is calling you home.
Grace does not say:
“Keep the chains and call them freedom.”
Grace says:
“Come out.”
Grace does not say:
“Rewrite Scripture until your desires become holy.”
Grace says:
“Bring your desires to Jesus and let Him rewrite you.”
And perhaps that is the question beneath the question.
Not:
“Can I find someone in Scripture who did what I want to do?”
But:
“Lord Jesus, what do You want from me?”
Those are very different ways to approach the Bible.
One searches Scripture for permission.
The other searches Scripture for Christ.
One asks:
“How close can I get to the boundary?”
The other asks:
“How close can I get to Jesus?”
One says:
“Abraham did it.”
The other remembers:
Jesus is greater than Abraham.
One says:
“David did it.”
The other remembers:
Jesus is the greater Son of David.
One says:
“Solomon did it.”
The other remembers:
Jesus said One greater than Solomon had come.
Christ is not merely another biblical character standing beside the patriarchs.
He is Lord.
He is the One toward whom the story moves.
And when He speaks about marriage...
He points us back to the beginning.
Male and female.
The two.
One flesh.
Covenant.
Faithfulness.
So can Christians use Old Testament polygamy to defend modern polygamy?
They can certainly point out that polygamy existed among important Old Testament figures.
They can correctly observe that Mosaic law regulated situations in which it occurred.
They can rightly insist that we must not fabricate biblical condemnations where Scripture itself speaks more carefully.
But none of those observations establishes polygamy as God's creational ideal or as the pattern Christ gives His disciples for marriage.
The stronger biblical case moves in the opposite direction.
Genesis establishes the one-flesh union.
The narratives repeatedly reveal the anguish surrounding divided households.
The Law restrains abuses without presenting multiplication of wives as the goal.
Israel's kings are warned not to multiply wives.
Solomon becomes the catastrophic example of that warning.
Jesus returns marriage to creation and explicitly speaks of “the two” becoming one flesh.
Paul again uses Genesis to describe Christian marriage and then points beyond marriage to Christ and the Church.
That is the context.
That is the trajectory.
And that is why Christians should never be frightened by difficult Bible passages.
Study them.
Open them.
Read what comes before.
Read what comes after.
Learn enough Hebrew and Greek to ask better questions, but never use ancient languages as decorations to make weak arguments sound scholarly.
Compare Scripture with Scripture.
And above everything...
look for Jesus.
Because sometimes the scandal is not that the Bible contains broken families.
The miracle is that God refused to abandon them.
Think about that.
Jesus' human genealogy runs through an astonishingly complicated history.
Broken households.
Sexual scandal.
Widowhood.
Outsiders.
Moral failure.
Kings with blood on their hands.
Families carrying secrets.
And through that human wreckage...
the Savior came.
Not to baptize the wreckage.
To redeem sinners from it.
That is why Gospel Warrior will never preach perfection as the entrance requirement for grace.
We preach Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.

If this exposed something hidden in you—not merely about polygamy, but about lust, faithfulness, marriage, secret compromise, or the way you have been using Scripture to defend something Jesus is asking you to surrender—be honest.
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop pretending the Word did not reach us.
Let believers see you.
Let somebody pray.
No more hiding.
Somebody reading silently may need evidence that grace still walks into ruined rooms.
You cannot purchase God's approval with engagement.
Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.

But if this truth can protect a marriage, confront a compromise, answer a skeptic, help a confused believer read Scripture faithfully, or bring one wandering person back toward Jesus, then sharing it can become a small act of Christian witness.
Even send it to the skeptic who thinks Christians are afraid of the difficult parts of their own Bible.
Because this argument will come again.
And when it does, don't answer with anger.
Open Scripture.
Follow.
Stay close to truth.
It doesn't.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, worship, love and faithful stewardship.
But supporting sound Gospel ministry can be one practical way of helping biblical teaching reach people who desperately need it.
Jesus is the treasure.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not merchandise.
Not religious content.
Jesus.
If supporting this ministry helps more people encounter His Word, praise God.
If sharing this article places truth in front of one wounded marriage, one confused Christian, one skeptic, one prodigal, one person secretly drowning in sexual compromise...
Perhaps someone has been searching for permission when what they really need is repentance.
Perhaps someone thinks their complicated history has disqualified them from grace.
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them the Bible does not hide broken families.
Tell them God entered them.
Tell them Abraham was imperfect.
Jacob's house was messy.
David fell terribly.
Solomon wandered catastrophically.
Peter denied Christ.
And still...
the Gospel moved forward.
Because redemption was never resting on their perfection.
It was resting on God's promise.
And ultimately that promise had a name.
Jesus Christ.
The Bridegroom.
The Savior.
The King.
The One who does not merely defend God's design...
but restores broken people who have violated it.
So don't use the failures of biblical men to lower the standard until it fits your desires.
Bring your desires to the feet of the perfect Man.
Bring Him your marriage.
Bring Him your sexuality.
Bring Him your fantasies.
Bring Him your wounds.
Bring Him your failures.
Bring Him the chapter you wish you could tear out of your life.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Seek wise pastoral and professional help where wounds are deep.
Protect the vulnerable.
Tell the truth.
And follow Jesus.
Because the greatest miracle of Scripture was never that God found perfect families.
It was that He kept walking through broken ones until He brought the Savior into the world.
And maybe that is exactly what somebody reading this needed tonight.
Your scandal may explain yesterday—but once surrendered to Jesus, it does not have the authority to write your ending.
